title: Does Sleep Help a Hangover? What Sleeping It Off Really Does
excerpt: Does sleep help a hangover? What sleeping it off actually does and does not do, why sleep after drinking is so poor, how long to sleep, naps, and when sleeping it off is not safe.
metaDescription: Does sleep help a hangover? What sleeping it off really does, why sleep after drinking is poor, how long to sleep, and when it is not safe to sleep it off.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** yes, sleep helps a hangover, but not in the way most people think. Sleep doesn't speed up how fast your liver clears alcohol, and it doesn't "sweat out" toxins. What it does is give your body time. A hangover is mostly something you wait out, and hours spent asleep are hours you don't spend feeling awful. Sleep also helps repay some of the rest that alcohol stole from you during the night, and poor sleep is one of the main reasons hangovers feel as bad as they do. So a few extra hours in bed the next morning usually makes a real difference.

The catch is the night itself. Sleep after drinking is lighter, more broken, and less restful than normal sleep, even when it feels like you were "out cold." And "sleeping it off" has a dangerous side: someone who has drunk a large amount should never be left alone to sleep it off, because blood alcohol can keep rising after they pass out.

**The quick rules:** Sleep in if you can. Drink a glass or two of water before bed and keep some by the bed. Stop drinking a few hours before you plan to sleep if you want the sleep to count. Don't take sleeping pills or sedating medicines on top of alcohol. And if someone is very drunk, can't be woken, is breathing slowly or irregularly, or is vomiting while barely conscious, that is not a person who needs sleep. That's a person who needs 911.

> **When to see a doctor or get help now.** This article is general information for social drinkers, not medical advice. **Call 911 (or your local emergency number) if someone** can't be woken up, is breathing slowly or with long gaps between breaths, has blue or very pale skin, feels cold to the touch, has a seizure, or is vomiting while passed out or barely responsive. These are signs of alcohol poisoning, and sleep won't fix them. **See a doctor soon if** your hangover symptoms last well beyond a day, you have chest pain, a racing or irregular heartbeat that won't settle, severe or one-sided headache, confusion, or you can't keep fluids down. **Talk to a doctor if** you regularly feel shaky, sweaty, anxious, or unable to sleep when you go a day without drinking. Those can be signs of alcohol withdrawal, which can be serious, and it's worth getting checked rather than pushing through it on your own.

## Does Sleep Help a Hangover? What Actually Happens

To see why sleep helps, it's useful to know what a hangover actually is. Researchers still argue about the details, but most agree a hangover comes from several things happening at once:

- **Your immune system reacting.** Heavy drinking triggers an inflammatory response, the same kind of signaling that makes you feel run down when you have a cold. Several studies have linked higher levels of these inflammation signals to worse hangover symptoms.
- **Acetaldehyde and other by-products.** When your liver breaks down alcohol, it first turns it into acetaldehyde, a toxic compound, before turning that into harmless acetate. Darker drinks also contain extra compounds called congeners that may add to the misery.
- **Fluid and stomach problems.** Alcohol makes you pee more and irritates your stomach lining.
- **Low blood sugar and disrupted body chemistry** in some people.
- **Bad sleep.** Alcohol wrecks the structure of your sleep, and much of the next-day tiredness, foggy thinking, and low mood comes from that alone.

A hangover usually starts when your blood alcohol drops back toward zero and can last up to about 24 hours. Sleep helps with several of these pieces:

1. **It lets time pass.** This is the biggest one. Most hangover symptoms fade on their own as your body finishes clearing alcohol and its by-products and as the inflammatory response calms down. Sleeping through part of that window means you're awake for less of it.
2. **It pays back sleep debt.** Because the sleep you got while drunk was poor, a few hours of more normal sleep the next morning can help the tiredness and brain fog that make up a big part of how a hangover feels.
3. **It gives your stomach a break.** Lying still and not eating or drinking anything irritating for a few hours can let nausea settle.
4. **Sleep supports recovery in general.** Your body does a lot of repair and immune regulation during sleep. That's true of recovering from any kind of stress, including a night of drinking.

What sleep doesn't do:

- **It doesn't make you sober faster.** Your liver clears alcohol at a fairly steady rate, very roughly one standard drink per hour for many people, whether you're asleep, awake, drinking coffee, or taking a cold shower.
- **It doesn't replace fluids.** You lose water overnight and wake up drier than you went to bed. Sleep is not a substitute for drinking water.
- **It doesn't "cure" anything.** If you wake up and still feel bad, that's normal. Most of a hangover simply has to run its course.

### What the research says about sleep and hangover severity

Researchers who study hangovers have looked at the link between sleep and how bad people feel the next day. Survey studies of drinkers have found that shorter and poorer sleep after drinking tends to go along with worse hangovers, and lab studies have shown that alcohol before bed reduces sleep quality and increases next-day sleepiness. A well-known 2013 review in *Alcoholism: Clinical and Experimental Research* (Ebrahim and colleagues, "Alcohol and sleep I") pulled together decades of lab work and found a consistent pattern: alcohol helps you fall asleep faster and deepens sleep early in the night, then disrupts sleep in the second half.

It's hard to fully separate cause and effect here. People who sleep less after drinking often also drank more or stayed out later. But the overall direction of the evidence is clear enough: better sleep is linked to a milder hangover, and alcohol makes it harder to get that sleep.

## Why Sleep After Drinking Is So Bad

Alcohol is a sedative, so it makes sense that people think it helps them sleep. It does help you fall asleep. The trouble comes later in the night. Our guide on [why alcohol makes you sleepy](/never-hungover/why-does-alcohol-make-you-sleepy) explains the first half of this story. Here's what happens next.

### The first half of the night: heavy and deep

As alcohol rises in your blood, it boosts the calming effects of GABA, the brain's main "slow down" chemical, and dampens excitatory signals. You fall asleep faster than usual, and the first part of the night tends to have more deep, slow-wave sleep. This is the "out like a light" feeling.

### The second half of the night: the rebound

As your liver clears the alcohol, your brain swings the other way. It had adjusted to the sedative, and now that the sedative is leaving, it ends up more alert than normal. This is often called a rebound effect. The result:

- **More waking up**, often in the early hours, sometimes without remembering it.
- **Lighter, more broken sleep.**
- **Less REM sleep overall**, and a burst of it late in the night once alcohol is gone, which can come with vivid dreams or nightmares.
- **Sweating, a racing heart, and feeling hot**, as your body's stress system kicks in.
- **Trips to the bathroom**, because alcohol makes you pee more.

REM sleep is the stage linked to dreaming, mood, and memory. Losing it is one reason you can feel emotionally flat or anxious the day after drinking. Our deeper explainer on [alcohol and REM sleep](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-rem-sleep-complete-scientific-analysis-2025) goes through what researchers have found. If you often wake at 3 or 4 a.m. after a night out and can't get back to sleep, our guide on [why you can't sleep after drinking](/never-hungover/cant-sleep-after-drinking) covers that pattern in detail.

### Other things that disrupt the night

- **Snoring and breathing problems.** Alcohol relaxes the muscles of your throat, which makes snoring worse and can worsen sleep apnea, the condition where breathing repeatedly stops and starts during sleep.
- **Acid reflux.** Alcohol relaxes the valve at the top of your stomach, so acid can creep up when you lie flat.
- **Late-night food and noise.** Real nights out often end late, in a hot or noisy room, after a heavy meal. Those all chip away at sleep too.
- **Going to bed too late.** If you get home at 3 a.m. and have to be up at 8, you've lost hours before alcohol even gets involved.

All of this means the sleep you get while drinking isn't worth as much as the same number of hours sober. Eight hours after a big night might feel like five.

## Is "Sleeping It Off" Safe?

For a person who had a few drinks and is tired, going to bed is perfectly fine. "Sleeping it off" becomes dangerous when someone has drunk a large amount, especially quickly.

### Blood alcohol can keep rising after you fall asleep

Alcohol takes time to be absorbed from the stomach and intestine. If someone drank a lot in a short period, especially shots or drinking games, their blood alcohol can keep climbing for a while after their last drink, even after they pass out. The person who "just needs to sleep" can be heading toward alcohol poisoning while they lie there.

### Choking on vomit is a real risk

Heavy drinking can cause vomiting, and alcohol dulls the gag reflex. Someone who is passed out on their back can vomit and inhale it. This is one of the ways people die from alcohol poisoning.

### Signs this is alcohol poisoning, not a person who needs sleep

The US National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism (NIAAA) lists these as critical signs of alcohol overdose:

- Mental confusion or stupor
- Difficulty staying conscious, or being unable to wake up
- Vomiting
- Seizures
- Slow breathing (fewer than about 8 breaths a minute) or irregular breathing (10 seconds or more between breaths)
- Slow heart rate
- Clammy skin, blue-tinged or very pale skin
- Low body temperature
- Dulled responses, such as no gag reflex

A person doesn't need to have all of these. If you're worried, call 911. Don't wait for every symptom to show up, and don't worry about overreacting. Emergency teams would much rather see someone who turns out to be fine.

### If you're looking after someone who's very drunk

If someone is drunk but awake, talking, and breathing normally, and you've decided they can go to bed, a few simple steps make it safer:

- **Put them on their side**, not their back, with their top knee bent forward so they don't roll over. This is the recovery position. It keeps the airway clear if they vomit.
- **Don't leave them alone.** Stay with them, or check on them often, and make sure you can wake them.
- **Don't give them a cold shower, coffee, or more alcohol.** None of these sober anyone up, and a cold shower can make low body temperature worse or cause a fall.
- **Don't try to make them walk it off.** Falls are a real risk.
- **If they get worse or you can't wake them, call 911.**

### It doesn't make you safe to drive

You might wake up feeling okay and still have alcohol in your blood. After a heavy night that ended late, it's very possible to be over the legal driving limit the next morning. Sleep doesn't speed up how fast alcohol leaves your body. If you drank a lot late into the night, plan for the morning: a later start, a ride, or public transport.

## How Much Sleep Do You Need to Get Over a Hangover?

There's no magic number, and anyone who gives you one is guessing. A few things are useful to know:

- **Most adults need about 7 to 9 hours a night** normally. After drinking, you'll likely need more time in bed to get the same amount of real rest, because some of the night was wasted on light, broken sleep.
- **Hangovers usually peak around the time your blood alcohol hits zero** and fade over the rest of the day. Our guide on [how long a hangover lasts](/never-hungover/how-long-does-hangover-last) breaks down the timeline and what affects it.
- **Sleeping in for a couple of extra hours is usually worth it** if your schedule allows. You're more likely to wake up after the worst of the symptoms has passed.

That said, there's a limit. Sleeping until mid-afternoon can leave you groggy, throw off your body clock, and make it harder to sleep that night, which can drag the after-effects into the next day. A reasonable middle ground for many people: sleep in a bit, get up, drink water, eat something gentle, get some daylight, and take a short nap later if you need it.

## Is a Nap Good for a Hangover?

A nap can help, especially if you were up late or woke early and couldn't get back to sleep. Some tips:

- **Keep it short or keep it long.** A 20 to 30 minute nap can refresh you without leaving you groggy. A longer nap of around 90 minutes lets you go through a full sleep cycle. Waking up from deep sleep in the middle, at around 45 to 60 minutes, often leaves you feeling worse for a while.
- **Nap earlier in the day.** A late-afternoon or evening nap can make it hard to fall asleep at night, which sets you up for a second rough night.
- **Drink some water before you lie down**, and have some nearby.
- **Eat first if you're hungry.** Low blood sugar can make you feel shaky and headachy, and food can help settle a hangover stomach.

## Should You Sleep In or Get Up and Move?

Both camps have a point. If you can sleep, sleep is probably the single best thing you can do for a typical hangover. If you're awake and can't drift back off, lying in bed staring at the ceiling isn't helping much.

If you can't sleep, here's what tends to help the most:

- **Water and electrolytes.** Rehydrating won't cure a hangover by itself, but it helps with thirst, dry mouth, and some headaches. Our guide to [electrolytes before or after drinking](/never-hungover/electrolytes-before-or-after-drinking) covers when they're worth it.
- **Bland food.** Toast, bananas, eggs, crackers, or soup.
- **Daylight and fresh air.** A short walk outside can help reset your body clock after a late night and may lift your mood.
- **Gentle movement only.** A walk or light stretching is fine. Hard exercise while you're dehydrated and your heart is still racing isn't a great idea.
- **Caffeine, in moderation.** A cup of coffee can help with grogginess if you normally drink it, and skipping it can add a caffeine-withdrawal headache. Too much can upset your stomach and make anxiety worse, and caffeine late in the day will hurt that night's sleep.

## Can You Take Something to Help You Sleep After Drinking?

This is where people get into trouble, so it's worth being direct.

- **Don't combine alcohol with sleeping pills or other sedatives.** Prescription sleep medicines, benzodiazepines, opioid painkillers, and some other drugs add to the sedating effect of alcohol. Together they can slow breathing to dangerous levels. Talk to your doctor or pharmacist about any medicine you take regularly and whether it's safe with alcohol.
- **Be careful with over-the-counter "PM" products.** Sleep aids and night-time cold medicines usually contain a sedating antihistamine such as diphenhydramine or doxylamine. Alcohol plus these can leave you more impaired and groggy than you expect. Many "PM" products also contain acetaminophen, which is a separate concern after drinking.
- **Melatonin** is a lot milder, but there's little research on taking it with alcohol, and it won't undo the sleep disruption alcohol causes. Our guide on [melatonin and alcohol](/never-hungover/melatonin-and-alcohol) covers what's known and the sensible precautions.
- **Don't drink more to get back to sleep.** "Hair of the dog" or a nightcap at 4 a.m. just restarts the cycle and pushes the hangover later.

If you regularly need a drink to fall asleep, or can't sleep without one, that's worth mentioning to a doctor. Alcohol tends to make sleep worse over time, not better, and there are good options for sleep problems that don't involve it.

## How to Get Better Sleep After Drinking

You can't make alcohol-affected sleep perfect, but you can make it a lot better. Most of these steps happen before bed.

### On the night

- **Stop drinking a few hours before bed.** The closer to bedtime you drink, the more alcohol is still in your system as you sleep, and the more of the night is hit by the rebound. A common rule of thumb is to finish your last drink around three hours before sleep, though more time is better after a bigger night.
- **Pace yourself.** Alternating alcoholic drinks with water slows you down and means less alcohol overall.
- **Eat a proper meal.** Food slows how quickly alcohol is absorbed and can make the peak less sharp.
- **Drink water before bed** and keep a glass or bottle by the bed. You'll probably wake up thirsty.
- **Use the bathroom before bed** to cut down on one wake-up.
- **Make the room cool, dark, and quiet.** Alcohol can make you run hot and sweaty in the second half of the night. Earplugs and an eye mask help if your sleep will already be fragile.
- **Sleep on your side** if you snore or tend to get reflux. Raising the head of the bed slightly can help with heartburn.
- **Skip the late-night greasy food if reflux is a problem for you.** A heavy meal right before lying down makes heartburn more likely.

### The next morning

- **Sleep in if you can.**
- **Drink water as soon as you wake.**
- **Eat something gentle.**
- **Get some daylight.**
- **Nap early and briefly if you need to.**
- **Go to bed at a normal time that night** so you don't carry the disruption into the next day.

### The most reliable fix

The step that helps sleep the most is the least exciting one: drink less. Fewer drinks, spread out, finished earlier, mean less alcohol in your system at bedtime and a smaller rebound. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) goes through the habits with the best evidence.

## Does It Matter What You Drink?

To some extent. Darker drinks like bourbon, brandy, and red wine contain more congeners than clear drinks like vodka, and a well-known study from Rohsenow and colleagues (published in *Alcoholism: Clinical and Experimental Research* in 2010) found that bourbon produced somewhat worse hangovers than vodka at the same blood alcohol level. In that same study, alcohol of either kind disrupted sleep compared with a placebo drink. So the type of drink may change how bad the hangover is a little, but the amount of alcohol you drink matters far more for your sleep.

Caffeinated mixers are worth a mention too. Energy drinks and cola mixed with alcohol can keep you up later and make it harder to fall asleep once you get home, on top of the alcohol's own effects.

## Where DHM Fits In

Some people use supplements to try to make the morning after easier. DHM (dihydromyricetin) is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree that has been studied for its effects on alcohol and the brain. In animal research, it appeared to counter some of alcohol's effects on GABA receptors, the same system involved in alcohol's sedating effect and the rebound later in the night. Lab work has also looked at its effects on how the liver processes alcohol.

It's important to be honest about the limits. Most of that evidence comes from animal and lab studies, and human research on DHM for hangovers is limited. There is no good evidence that DHM prevents hangovers, and it doesn't make drunk sleep normal, sober you up faster, or make it safe to drive. It won't replace sleep, water, food, or simply drinking less.

If you'd like to try it, people usually take it with their drinks or before bed. Popular picks include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the lower-cost [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much people take and when. If you take any prescription medicines, check with your doctor or pharmacist before adding a new supplement.

## The Bottom Line

- **Yes, sleep helps a hangover.** It lets time pass, makes up some of the rest alcohol took from you, and lets your body recover. Sleeping in is one of the most useful things you can do.
- **Sleep doesn't sober you up faster** and doesn't replace water or food.
- **Sleep while drunk is poor sleep.** Alcohol helps you fall asleep, then disrupts the second half of the night with waking, lighter sleep, and less REM.
- **Finishing your last drink a few hours before bed** and drinking water before you sleep are the simplest ways to sleep better after a night out.
- **"Sleeping it off" is not safe for someone who is very drunk.** If a person can't be woken, is breathing slowly or irregularly, is vomiting while barely conscious, or has a seizure, call 911.
- **Don't mix alcohol with sleeping pills or sedating medicines.**

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Does sleep help a hangover?**

Yes. Sleep doesn't speed up how fast your body clears alcohol, but it lets you get through part of the hangover without feeling it, helps make up for the poor sleep you got while drinking, and supports your body's recovery. Sleeping in a couple of extra hours is usually worth it if you can.

**Can you sleep off a hangover?**

Partly. Most hangovers fade on their own over the course of a day, so sleeping through some of that time means you feel less of it. You may still wake up with a headache, thirst, or tiredness, so drink water and eat something gentle when you get up. Sleeping into the afternoon can leave you groggy and make it harder to sleep that night.

**Does sleeping sober you up?**

No. Your liver clears alcohol at a fairly steady rate, very roughly one standard drink per hour for many people, whether you're asleep or awake. After a heavy night that ended late, you may still have alcohol in your blood the next morning, even after a full night's sleep, and may not be safe to drive.

**Is it safe to let a drunk person sleep it off?**

Only if they're awake enough to talk, breathing normally, and able to be woken. Put them on their side in the recovery position, stay with them or check on them often, and never leave them alone if they're very drunk. Blood alcohol can keep rising after someone passes out. If they can't be woken, are breathing slowly or irregularly, have blue or pale skin, feel cold, have a seizure, or are vomiting while barely conscious, call 911.

**Why do I sleep badly after drinking?**

Alcohol helps you fall asleep and deepens sleep early in the night, but as your body clears it, your brain rebounds into a more alert state. That leads to more waking, lighter sleep, less REM sleep, sweating, a faster heart rate, and bathroom trips in the second half of the night. Snoring and acid reflux can make it worse.

**How long should I sleep to get rid of a hangover?**

There's no set number. Most adults need 7 to 9 hours normally, and after drinking you'll probably need more time in bed to get the same rest. Sleeping in for a couple of hours often helps, but sleeping very late can throw off your body clock. A short nap earlier in the day is a good backup.

**Is it better to sleep or stay awake with a hangover?**

If you can sleep, sleep is usually the better choice. If you're awake and can't drift off, get up, drink water, eat something bland, and get some daylight. A short walk is fine, but skip hard exercise until you feel better.

**Can I take a sleeping pill after drinking?**

It's not a good idea. Sleeping pills, benzodiazepines, opioid painkillers, and sedating antihistamines in "PM" products all add to alcohol's sedating effect and can slow breathing. Talk to your doctor or pharmacist about any medicine you take regularly and whether it's safe with alcohol.

**Does DHM help you sleep better after drinking?**

There's no good evidence that DHM makes sleep after drinking normal or prevents hangovers. Animal research suggests it may counter some of alcohol's effects on the brain's GABA system, which is involved in alcohol's sedating effect, but human research is limited. It doesn't replace sleep, water, food, or drinking less.
